volumes.title: The Carrier’s Cart
volumes.text:
I am Tamsin Rudd, piano tuner, of Tallow Lane in Emberwick, and until Tuesday the highest thing I had climbed was the organ loft at the chapel. Then came a letter from Mrs Hallam of Kettledale Head. Her piano had not been tuned in eleven years, her daughter Bess was to be married on Saturday, and would I come.

By road Kettledale is two days round through the Lowlands. Over the High Pass it is nine miles. I chose the nine miles. I say this so that nobody else is blamed.

The carrier set me down at Gimmer Gate, the last farm, at seven. The fell postman was waiting there with his bag: Osric Mattock, a lean man the colour of a fence. He looked at my tuning case, then at my boots. “Nine miles,” he said, “and two thousand feet. The feet are the long part.”

volumes.title: The First Thousand Feet
volumes.text:
From Gimmer Gate the path to the High Pass goes straight up beside Scrat Beck, and it does not apologise. I am a piano tuner, and had imagined a pass as a kind of lane. Osric Mattock, the fell postman, who crosses every Tuesday with the Kettledale bag and comes back on Thursday, walked ahead at the pace of a man following a hearse.

I thought him slow. I passed him twice in the first half hour, and twice sat down on a rock with my heart going like a metronome set too fast, and twice he went by without a word or a change of step. After the second time I fell in behind him and stayed there.

By nine the farm was a grey button below us, and my tuning case, eleven pounds in Emberwick, weighed nearer twenty. Osric said it would be thirty at the top.

volumes.title: A Summit That Wasn’t
volumes.text:
At half past nine on the morning I crossed the High Pass, I reached the top. There was a cairn on a green shoulder and nothing above it but sky. I put down my tuning case, shook the postman’s hand, and ate both my sandwiches as a celebration.

Osric Mattock let me finish. He is a patient man; he has carried the Kettledale post over this fell every Tuesday for twenty-six years. Then he pointed with his stick. Behind the green shoulder stood the rest of the mountain, grey, steep, and a good deal taller than the part we had done. A thin path wandered up into a notch between two crags.

“That’s the pass,” he said. “This is Hopeful Knott. Everybody eats their dinner here.” I had one apple left for the real dinner hour, and I have thought about those sandwiches a great deal.

volumes.title: Weather From the West
volumes.text:
Above Hopeful Knott, on the long slant up to the High Pass, Osric Mattock stopped for the first time all morning. He is the fell postman, and I was the piano tuner he had agreed to see over to Kettledale. He sniffed. He looked west, where the sky had gone the colour of a pewter plate. “Ten minutes,” he said, and got his cape out.

It was eight. The rain came up the valley like a curtain being drawn, and then it was simply everywhere: in front, behind, and blowing upward. I had a good town mackintosh. It kept the rain off very well in all the places where the rain was not trying to get in. The rest came down my neck in a steady, exploring trickle.

I asked how long it would last. Osric considered the matter fairly. “It’s Tuesday now,” he said.

volumes.title: The Peat Hags
volumes.text:
Two thirds of the way up to the High Pass the ground gives up being ground. The path crosses a wide black shelf of peat, cut into islands and trenches, and every trench holds water the colour of strong tea. Osric Mattock, the postman, went over it in a zigzag, like a man who knows which stair creaks. I, Tamsin Rudd, piano tuner, followed three steps behind and one step wrong.

My left leg went in to the knee. It was not dangerous. It was only cold, and extremely firm. Osric came back and took my tuning case from me first, I noticed, and then my arm. The bog let go with a noise like a cork leaving a very large bottle. My boot came too, which he said was lucky.

“It has a pair of mine,” he said. “From my first winter. I expect it’s keeping them for me.”

volumes.title: The Shelter Stone
volumes.text:
Halfway over the High Pass, by Osric Mattock’s reckoning, there is a boulder the size of a hay cart that leans on another. Underneath is a dry space with room for a postman, a piano tuner, and one sheep who was there first and did not move up.

We ate. That is, Osric ate oatcake and cold bacon, and I ate an apple, having finished my sandwiches hours too soon on Hopeful Knott. He watched me for a while, then broke the oatcake down the middle and handed half across without remark. It was the best thing I have eaten this year.

I took stock. Hat: wet. Collar: wet. Left leg: peat to the knee. The Kettledale letters, wrapped in oilcloth in his bag, were perfectly dry. I said the post was better looked after than the passenger. “The post can’t walk,” said Osric, and gave the sheep his crust.

volumes.title: Into the Cloud
volumes.text:
Above the shelter stone the High Pass goes into the cloud and does not come out until the other side. I could see my own boots, the postman’s back, and sometimes a cairn: a heap of stones as tall as a child, looming grey out of the grey. There is one every forty paces. Osric Mattock built eleven of them himself.

We went from cairn to cairn like people crossing a dark room by the furniture. My legs had stopped complaining and begun simply to report: this is a step, this is another.

At every cairn Osric whistled one low note. I asked why. For Fly, he said, a dog he had for fourteen years; she used to wait at each one. I am a piano tuner. The note was a flat B, every time, exactly the same flat B. I have known pianos less reliable.

volumes.title: The Top of the Pass
volumes.text:
The top of the High Pass is a notch between two crags, about as wide as Tallow Lane at home, with the wind coming through it like a train. I reached it at ten past one behind Osric Mattock, the fell postman, and sat down on the first thing that was not a puddle.

There is a slate box there, built into the rock, with a flat stone for a lid. Kettledale folk leave their letters in it and Osric collects them: four that day, and a parcel of knitting. He wrote the time in a small book.

I had hoped for a view. There was cloud. Then, for about as long as it takes to say so, it tore open, and I saw a green valley far down, a beck like a dropped thread, and one white farm. “Kettledale Head,” said Osric. “That’s your piano.” Then it shut.

volumes.title: Downhill Is Not Easier
volumes.text:
I had supposed, all the way up the High Pass, that the way down would be a rest. I mention it as a warning. The Kettledale side falls away in a slope of loose slate, and the path goes down it in zigzags, forty-one of them. I counted. Counting was the only part of me still working.

Going up, it is the lungs that object. Going down it is the knees, then the toes, which arrive at the front of each boot a moment before the rest of you. My tuning case swung round and knocked me behind the legs at every turn, like a child wanting attention.

Osric Mattock, the postman, went down ahead with his hands behind his back, as a man goes down his own stairs. At the bottom he waited. “Now,” he said kindly, “it’s only walking.” It was three miles of only walking.

volumes.title: Five Stepping Stones
volumes.text:
There are five stepping stones over Kettle Beck, a mile above the farm where I was to tune a piano. By then I had crossed the High Pass in rain, bog and cloud, and I looked at those stones with contempt. Osric Mattock, the postman, went over first. He said, without turning round, “Mind the fourth.”

I minded the third very carefully. The fourth turned under me like a loaf in a tin, and I sat down in the beck.

It was up to my waist and astonishingly cold, and the odd thing is that I laughed, because there was nothing left to get wet. I found I was holding my tuning case above my head in both hands, quite dry. Osric took it and looked it over with approval. “That’s the trade showing,” he said. Then he gave me his arm, for the second time that day.

volumes.title: Kettledale Head
volumes.text:
We came down to Kettledale Head at a quarter to five, the fell postman and I, nine miles and one beck after leaving Gimmer Gate. Mrs Hallam met us in the yard, took Osric Mattock’s letters with one hand and me with the other, and said, “You poor wet thing, you came over the top.”

Within ten minutes I was in the kitchen in a flannel shirt and a pair of Mr Hallam’s trousers, rolled up five times at the ankle and held with string. My own clothes steamed on the rack over the range. There was mutton broth with barley, and I ate as a tuner should not in front of a client.

The piano stood in the parlour. I meant to try one note, just the A. I woke at the table an hour later with a blanket round me, and Osric gone on his round.

volumes.title: The Piano at Last
volumes.text:
On Wednesday morning at Kettledale Head I came downstairs sideways, holding the rail. Crossing the High Pass had found muscles I had not been told about. But a tuner works sitting down, and Mrs Hallam’s piano had waited eleven years.

It was a full half-tone flat, every string, all in fair agreement, like a valley that has kept its own time because nobody came over to correct it. I had it up to pitch by four. Bess Hallam, who is to be married on Saturday, played a polka, and her mother stood in the doorway with flour on her hands and forgot the baking.

Osric Mattock, the fell postman, crosses again tomorrow and I am going with him. Mr Hallam has offered the cart round by the Lowlands. I thanked him. I find I should like to see Hopeful Knott from above, and to mind the fourth stone.

volumes.title: Rules of the Hut
volumes.text:
This book belongs to Bield Hut on Scrat Fell and stops here. It is kept in the tin on the shelf, out of the way of mice.

April 2nd. I am Abel Wren, shepherd to Mr Tolley of Gimmer Gate. I am up here most days at lambing and not many after. Others use the hut and are welcome. I have never known who. So write your name, the weather, and what you burned. Leave kinling as you found it. Latch the door or the ewes get in. There is one spoon. It stays. Weather today: cold, east wind, bright. Lambs so far: fourteen. Burned: four peats.

April 6th, Sunday. Miss P. Quill, Emberwick, walking. Fine, with larks. Burned nothing; ate a pie. I latched the door. Mr Wren, it is spelled kindling, with a d. I taught school for thirty years and cannot help it. A good hut.

volumes.title: Kindling, With a D
volumes.text:
The book of Bield Hut, Scrat Fell. April 9th. Sleet. Lambs: thirty-one. Burned six peats and the kindling, with a d. Fetched more. A. Wren, shepherd.

April 13th, Sunday. Showers, then a rainbow with both ends in the valley. I found the kindling box full and beside it a slate with KINDLING chalked on it, correctly. I am answered. I have left a quarter of tea in the tin, as a peace offering. P. Quill, walking from Emberwick.

April 15th. Dry. Lambs: fifty-two, and twins on the scree, which is a daft place. Tea found. I make it stronger than you would, I expect. A. Wren. April 16. Ned Tolley, age 9. I came up with Abel. I carried a lamb all the way from the gill and it went to sleep. It is not ritten in the rules but I ate my dinner with the spoon.

volumes.title: A Hole Above the Stove
volumes.text:
Bield Hut book, Scrat Fell. May 4th, Sunday. Heavy rain from the west. There is a hole in the roof directly above the stove, which seems to me the one place a hut should not have one. I have set the bucket under it. Burned three peats. Mr Wren, the bucket will want emptying by Tuesday. P. Quill.

May 6th. Bucket emptied. I know about the hole. It has been there since the gale in March and so have two hundred and ten lambs, and the lambs come first. Lambing done Friday. Slates Saturday. A. Wren, shepherd.

May 8th. Josiah Hake, pedlar, crossing to Kettledale with ribbons and needles. Slept here dry by sitting in the corner away from the bucket. Burned two peats. Left a card of darning needles for the house, in thanks. The spoon is a good spoon.

volumes.title: Four New Slates
volumes.text:
May 11th, Sunday. Bright and cold. Bield Hut has a whole roof: four new slates, greyer than the old ones, and the bucket hung back on its nail. I sat under them for the pleasure of it. Mr Wren, thank you, on behalf of the public. I have brought up a second cup, since the book shows the hut now has callers. P. Quill, Emberwick.

May 14th. Fine. Sheep to the high ground. Cup noted. It is a better cup than the hut one, so I have been using it. There is a ring ouzel nesting in the gill forty yards above the door, left side, under the rowan. Go quiet and you will see her. A. Wren, shepherd.

May 18th, Sunday. I went quiet. I saw her. Four eggs, Mr Wren, blue-green and freckled. I taught thirty years of children about birds out of a book. P. Quill.

volumes.title: Clipping Week
volumes.text:
July 7th. Hot. Clipping at the fold below Bield Hut, six men and Ned. Two hundred and forty ewes shorn by Thursday if it holds dry. Burned nothing; nobody wants a fire. The hut smells of wool grease and will for a month. A. Wren, shepherd. July 8. Ned Tolley, 9 and three quarters. I rolled forty fleeces. My hands are soft now from the grease, like a lady’s, Abel says. I rote this at dinner time.

July 13th, Sunday. Warm, hazy. The hut does smell of sheep. I find I do not mind. Ned, it is wrote, with a w, but forty fleeces is a great many and I am impressed. I must report that the spoon is not on its nail. P. Quill, walking from Emberwick.

July 15th. Spoon gone. Thirty years it has hung there. I am not accusing the public. A. Wren.

volumes.title: The Matter of the Spoon
volumes.text:
Bield Hut, Scrat Fell: the book in the tin. August 3rd, Sunday. Thundery. No spoon. I stirred with a pencil. P. Quill.

August 5th. Two of us from the Grey Coast, Hal and Winnie Sark, walking the tops for a week. Came in out of a downpour that had us wet to the vest. Burned four peats, dried our stockings, and replaced the peats from the stack. We read the whole book while we waited. We did not take the spoon. We feel we ought to say so.

August 12th. Josiah Hake, pedlar, coming back from Kettledale. Read of the spoon. Have left a new one, tin, from my pack, no charge. It is not the same, I know. August 14th. New spoon hung up. Obliged to Mr Hake. It is not the same. A. Wren, shepherd.

volumes.title: Found in a Pocket
volumes.text:
September 6. Ned Tolley, nearly 10. I have to rite something. Wite. Write. My mother turned out my clipping jacket for the wash and the hut spoon was in the pocket. I did not steal it. I ate my dinner at the fold in July and put it there to bring back and forgot for eight weeks. I walked up by myself to hang it on the nail. Burned nothing. Weather windy.

September 7th, Sunday. A clear, cold morning; first frost on the rushes. Two spoons on the nail. Ned, you spelled write three ways and the third is right, and you walked two miles uphill to put a thing back. Full marks. P. Quill, in the Bield Hut book.

September 9th. Spoon home. Nobody was accused. The tin one can stay for company. Ned can carry the salt up Thursday, since he knows the way. A. Wren, shepherd.

volumes.title: The Autumn Gather
volumes.text:
October 11th. Bield Hut book, Scrat Fell. Three days gathering the fell for the autumn sales, in mist you could lean on. Gyp found the last nine ewes on Winnock Edge by nose alone. I found the hut the same way, near enough. Slept here two nights. Burned twelve peats and am not sorry. All down now. A. Wren, shepherd.

October 12th, Sunday. Still and grey, the bracken gone the colour of a fox. The fell is empty of sheep and looks larger without them. Six months of Sundays, Mr Wren, and I know your handwriting better than my sister’s. I have left a fruit loaf in the tin. It is for you and not for the public. P. Quill.

October 14th. Loaf found. Gyp had none of it. I write slower than I talk, Miss Quill, but I am glad of the book. A. W.

volumes.title: The Stove Laid Ready
volumes.text:
November 9th, Sunday. Rain all the way up from Emberwick and sleet for the last half mile. I am sixty-four. I reached Bield Hut wet to the knees, my hat brim running like a gutter, and found the stove laid ready: paper, kindling, three peats, and a match on top. Whoever does this, and I believe I know, has my thanks. Burned the three and laid three more. P. Quill.

November 12th. Hard frost. Up to look at the tups. I lay the stove on a Saturday now. It is no trouble. Days are short, Miss Quill; be off the fell by three, and take the cart track, not the gill. A. Wren, shepherd.

November 16th, Sunday. Bitter. Left by half past two, by the cart track, as instructed. I have not been told what to do in a long while. It was rather pleasant. P. Quill.

volumes.title: Snow to the Sill
volumes.text:
January 18th. This is the book of Bield Hut on Scrat Fell. I am Abel Wren, shepherd, and I am the only one in it this month. Snow to the window sill. Came up by the sledge track with hay for forty ewes sheltering in the hollow. Dug out the door. Burned eight peats. I read the book through from April while my stockings dried. It took one pipe. I had not thought a hut could have so much said in it.

January 25th. More snow, soft. Fed the ewes. No Sunday walker again, which is right and sensible. The hut is quiet without the handwriting. I have put her cup on the high shelf out of the frost. A. W.

February 2nd. Ned Tolley, 10. I came up on the sledge. Abel let me write the weather. It is drippy.

volumes.title: Four Leaves Left
volumes.text:
March 8th, Sunday. Mild, a wind that smelled of earth. I am back at Bield Hut after ten Sundays kept in Emberwick by the snow, and walked up slower than in autumn. My cup was on the high shelf, wrapped in a sock. I read January. Mr Wren, I missed the hut too. P. Quill.

March 11th. Bright. Ewes heavy; lambing in three weeks. I have counted the leaves left in this book and there are four. It was a sixpenny one. I never thought to fill it. A. Wren, shepherd.

March 15th, Sunday. Showers. The last page ought not to be wasted on weather. In eleven months we have never once been under this roof on the same day. I can walk on a weekday. Name one. P. Quill. March 17th. Second of April. It is a year to the day. Ned will want to come. A. W.

volumes.title: The Second of April
volumes.text:
April 2nd. The last page of the book of Bield Hut, Scrat Fell, begun a year ago today. All three of us are writing it at the one table, which is a squash. Weather: cold, bright, east wind, the same as the first page. Lambs so far: eleven. Burned five peats and boiled the kettle twice. Miss Quill is a deal taller than her handwriting. She brought a new book, a shilling one, with a red spine. It is in the tin. A. Wren, shepherd.

I was shown twin lambs an hour old, and the gill, where the ouzel is back and building. Mr Wren is exactly like his handwriting. We used both cups. P. Quill, Emberwick.

Ned Tolley, 10. I stirred everybodys tea with the old spoon. I spelled kindling for Miss Quill out loud. This book is full now. Write in the next one.

volumes.title: The Least of the Twelve
volumes.text:
No. 1. Butter Howe. 2,004 feet. Cairn: knee high, untidy. Weather: fair.

There is a list pinned up in the Emberwick Library of the twelve tops of the Northern Fells that stand over two thousand feet, lowest first. I am Cuthbert Pym, draper, retired this spring after forty years of measuring other people’s curtains, and I mean to stand on all twelve before the snow. I have a notebook, a tape, a yellow muffler my sister knitted, and twelve white pebbles from the Grey Coast, one for each cairn.

Butter Howe is the least of them, by four feet. It took me three hours and I lay down at the top. I measured the cairn, added pebble the first, and saw a slate tucked in on the lee side. Scratched with a nail: H.L., May 9th. Three days ago. I had rather thought I was the only one.

volumes.title: Stoat Nab in Drizzle
volumes.text:
No. 2. Stoat Nab. 2,060 feet. Cairn: waist high, well built, a credit to somebody. Weather: drizzle, of the fine sort that gets through tweed.

Second of the twelve tops on the library list, which I, C. Pym, late draper of Emberwick, am climbing in order, lowest first. The way up is by a sheep trod through bracken and then a grass slope the angle of a roof. I stopped eleven times. I have decided to record the stops honestly, since nobody will read this but me.

On top, nothing to see but the inside of a cloud. Cairn measured: thirty-eight inches. White pebble placed. And there on the sheltered side was a slate again, scratched H.L., May 17th. Five days ahead of me. The same hand, the same nail. Somebody else has read that list. I ate my bread and cheese with my back to it.

volumes.title: Shirtsleeves on Spindle Rigg
volumes.text:
No. 3. Spindle Rigg. 2,118 feet. Cairn: tall and thin, like its name; forty-six inches. Weather: hot, without a breath.

I am working through the twelve two-thousand-foot tops of the Northern Fells in the order of the library list, and this was the first done in shirtsleeves. Spindle Rigg is a long narrow ridge that you walk like a plank. The yellow muffler went in the knapsack. The first blister arrived at sixteen hundred feet, right heel, and is dressed with best lint from my own shop.

Slate on the lee side of the cairn: H.L., May 28th. I sat and considered H.L. A tall man, I think, from the time he gains on me. Young. Long in the leg. A Harold, or a Hubert. Probably he does not stop eleven times. Stops today: nine. Pebble placed. A lark sang the whole while, which was civil of it.

volumes.title: Hat Weather on Hagworm Pike
volumes.text:
No. 4. Hagworm Pike. 2,190 feet. Cairn: broad and squat, thirty inches; built by someone who understood wind. Weather: wind.

Fourth of my twelve tops, and the first with any rock to it. The name is the old word for an adder. I saw none. They had more sense than to be out. From the shoulder upward the wind came across so hard that I walked at a slant, like a man carrying a wardrobe, and at the top it took my hat clean off.

I, Cuthbert Pym, sixty-one, went after it on hands and knees. It had not gone to Kettledale, as I feared. It had lodged against the far side of the cairn, six inches from a slate scratched H.L., June 6th. I retrieved the one and glared at the other. Pebble placed, and wedged. Stops: I did not count. Standing still was harder than walking.

volumes.title: Lamb’s Lug, the Wet Way
volumes.text:
No. 5. Lamb’s Lug. 2,240 feet. Cairn: a poor heap, twenty inches, half sunk in moss. Weather: bright, after a week of rain, which is the worst of both.

A lug is an ear, and from Emberwick this fell looks like one, folded over. Close to, it is a sponge. I am Cuthbert Pym, retired draper, and this is the fifth of the twelve tops I have set myself. For two miles the ground quaked. I went in over one boot, then the other, and near the top I sat down suddenly in a green place that was not grass. I walked the rest wet from the waist, squelching in two different notes.

Slate at the cairn: H.L., June 15th. Dry-shod, no doubt. I added six stones out of charity and set my white pebble on top. Trousers dried on me by Gimmer Gate. Stops: fourteen, a record.

volumes.title: Lost on Scrat Fell
volumes.text:
No. 6. Scrat Fell. 2,305 feet. Cairn: large, round, shoulder high; fifty-two inches when at last measured. Weather: cloud down to the top wall.

Sixth of the twelve tops on the library list, and so the half of my summer’s task. The top of Scrat Fell is flat and as wide as Emberwick market square. In cloud, that is not a help. I, Cuthbert Pym, wandered on it for forty minutes, looking for a cairn the size of a haystack. I passed the same puddle three times and began to greet it.

I found the cairn by walking into it. I am not ashamed to say I patted it. Then round to the lee side, and there was the slate, H.L., June 24th, quite at home. For once I was almost pleased to see the fellow’s initials. Six pebbles placed. Six in the knapsack. Down by compass, slowly.

volumes.title: Two in One Day
volumes.text:
No. 7. Fiddler’s Knott. 2,350 feet. Cairn: neat, square-shouldered, forty inches. Weather: clear and cool, the best day of July.

I have been climbing the twelve high tops of the Northern Fells, lowest first, and at every cairn I find a slate scratched H.L., with a date some days before mine. Today’s said July 8th. Mine was the 12th. I ate a pork pie and looked across at the next on the list, Little Thunnock, a mile off along the ridge, with one dip between.

Not yet noon. A draper does not get to be sixty-one without knowing how to make up a short measure. If I did two tops in a day, I, Cuthbert Pym, should gain on a man who plainly does one. Pebble placed. Stops: seven. I wound my muffler twice round and set off into the dip, which was deeper than it looked.

volumes.title: Little Thunnock, Late
volumes.text:
No. 8. Little Thunnock. 2,410 feet. Cairn: about forty-four inches, measured sitting down. Weather: fine, then evening.

Eighth of the twelve tops, and my second in one day, which I do not recommend. The dip between Fiddler’s Knott and this one is five hundred feet down and, I can now state, a good eight hundred up again. I reached the cairn at ten past five with legs like two rolls of wet flannel. Stops: nineteen, the last one four yards from the top.

But the slate. H.L., July 11th. Yesterday! I, Cuthbert Pym, was four days behind at breakfast and one day behind at tea. I set down pebble the eighth, leaned back on the cairn to enjoy the moment, and woke twenty minutes later with a sheep looking at me. Home by lantern at ten. My sister had kept the stew hot and her remarks short.

volumes.title: Winnock Edge, Twice
volumes.text:
No. 9. Winnock Edge. 2,480 feet. Cairn: on the very lip, forty-one inches. Weather: first, rain like poured gravel; second, grey and still.

I, Cuthbert Pym, retired draper, have nine of the twelve tops, but this one I had to ask twice. The first time I thought I was a day behind H.L., whose slates I find at every cairn, and meant to catch him. At eighteen hundred feet the rain came on so hard I could not see my boots. I stood a minute, then turned round. It was the most sensible thing I have done since retiring. I was in a temper all the way down.

A week later I went back. The slate said July 20th: ten days ahead of me. I sat looking down on Ouzel Tarn and found I did not much mind. A list is not a race. Pebble placed. Stops: eight.

volumes.title: A Figure on Great Thunnock
volumes.text:
No. 10. Tinker’s Chair. 2,560 feet. Cairn: built inside the chair itself, a hollow of rock with two arms; thirty-six inches. Weather: perfect. I use the word once in this book.

Tenth of the twelve tops on the library list. The last day of August, heather in bloom the whole way up and the Grey Coast shining like a pin along the edge of everything. I, Cuthbert Pym, sat in the Tinker’s Chair for an hour and ate two apples. Slate present: H.L., August 19th.

Across the gap stands Great Thunnock, next on the list. Beside its cairn there was a small dark figure. It did not move for some time. Then something flashed, twice, as glass does. On an impulse I cannot defend, I stood and waved my yellow muffler over my head like a signalman. The figure waved back. Pebble placed. Stops: I forgot to count.

volumes.title: A Message on a Slate
volumes.text:
No. 11. Great Thunnock. 2,690 feet. Cairn: a massive beehive, sixty inches; the finest of the lot. Weather: cold wind, high cloud, the first smell of autumn.

Eleventh of the twelve high tops, and a hard pull of four hours from Gimmer Gate. I, Cuthbert Pym, am sixty-one and felt every one of the two thousand six hundred and ninety feet. I went round to the lee side of the cairn, as I have all summer, for the slate marked H.L.

It was a larger slate this time, scratched small: H.L., August 31st. To the gentleman in the yellow muffler who has been one fell behind me since May. I have watched you through my glass. You stop a great deal but you always get there. Ember Head, last Saturday in September, noon. I shall bring cake. I read it three times. Pebble placed, not quite straight.

volumes.title: Ember Head
volumes.text:
No. 12. Ember Head. 2,843 feet. Cairn: seven feet; my tape would not reach the top. Weather: clear, frost in the shadows.

The last and highest of the twelve tops. A spring comes out of the moss below the summit, no wider than a ribbon, and that is the river Ember. I, Cuthbert Pym, stepped over it and arrived at five minutes to noon.

H.L., whose slates I have found at eleven cairns, was sitting against this one with a spyglass and a cake tin. She is Miss Hetty Lumb, seventy-two, who kept the bakehouse in Oven Lane, and comes up to my shoulder. I had imagined a tall young man. We ate seed cake. She scratched C.P. under H.L. on the last slate, and I set down my twelfth pebble. Stops: twenty-two. She says the library has another list. Nineteen tarns. She has not started it yet.

volumes.title: Where the Cart Stops
volumes.text:
The carrier would go no farther than the last gate. He set Nell Garth down on the second of November with her box, pointed up the track, and turned for Emberwick before the light went.

Nell was eleven. Her mother had gone to the Lowlands to nurse a sister through the winter, and Nell had been sent to a great-aunt she had met twice. Above her the track climbed to a grey farm with one lit window. Below the farm lay a tarn, dark as a slate. Above that was only fell, and a good deal of that.

Great-Aunt Dinah came down to meet her, a small square woman in a sacking apron. She looked at Nell’s face, and then, for longer, at her boots. “Those won’t do,” she said. “The ouzel left three weeks back, so it’s winter. Come in. There’s broth.” She carried the box herself.

volumes.title: The Byre at Six
volumes.text:
At High Ouzel, the farm above the tarn, the day began in the dark. Nell Garth had been there one night when her great-aunt Dinah shook her foot through the blanket and said, “Six.” That was the whole of the conversation until the byre.

The byre was warm, which surprised her. It held a brown cow named Duchess, eleven hens, and an old dog called Captain, who had retired from sheep and now supervised. Nell carried two pails from the trough and slopped most of one down her stockings. She forked hay. She held the lantern while Dinah milked, and Duchess breathed on her hair.

By seven her arms shook when she lifted her porridge spoon. Dinah watched without comment and added more cream. Nell had found a stub of chalk on the byre sill and made one small mark inside the door. One day of winter done.

volumes.title: Aunt Dinah’s Clogs
volumes.text:
Nell Garth’s town boots lasted four days of her winter at High Ouzel. On the fifth, the left sole came away at the toe and flapped like a tongue across the yard. Her great-aunt Dinah heard it coming.

She said nothing. She went up to the loft and came down with a pair of clogs, black leather on alder soles, shod with iron like a pony. They had been hers at eleven, she said, and her mother’s before. With two pairs of stockings they fitted. Nell stood up in them and was an inch taller and a good deal louder. On the frozen ruts of the track she rang like a smithy.

Dinah tied the town boots together by their laces and hung them on a nail by the door. “For March,” she said. They hung there all winter above the tarn, looking smaller every time Nell passed.

volumes.title: The Tarn Skins Over
volumes.text:
The first ice came to Ouzel Tarn at the end of November. Nell Garth, eleven, who was wintering at the farm above it with her great-aunt Dinah, saw it from the yard: the water had stopped moving. A skin lay over it, clear at the edges and grey in the middle.

She was down the field before she had thought. Dinah’s voice came after her, not loud. “Not a foot on it till I say. I’ll say.” So Nell stood on the shore and threw a pebble instead. It did not splash. It skipped over the ice, and at every bounce the whole tarn chirped like a bird.

She threw until her fingers would not close. Dinah came down at last, picked up a flat stone, and sent it clear to the far side, ringing all the way. “Sixty years,” she said. “It never stops being worth doing.”

volumes.title: Counting to Sixty
volumes.text:
Before the snow, the ewes come down. Great-Aunt Dinah kept sixty small grey fell sheep at High Ouzel, and in the first week of December she, Nell Garth, who was eleven, and the old dog Captain brought them down into the walled field above the tarn.

It took all day. The wind had ice in it. Nell’s job was to stand in gaps and be a gate, which meant holding out her arms while sheep ran at her and thought better of it. By dusk she could not feel her ears, and her legs wobbled from walking on tussocks since breakfast.

Dinah counted them through the gate in fives, moving a pebble from one pocket to the other for every score. Three pebbles. Nell counted too, under her breath, and made it fifty-nine. Dinah pointed with her chin. The sixtieth was behind them, eating hay off the sledge.

volumes.title: The Shortest Day
volumes.text:
On the shortest day the sun cleared the fell above High Ouzel at half past nine and was gone behind it by three. Nell Garth, eleven, had been at her great-aunt Dinah’s farm seven weeks. The chalk marks she kept on the byre door, one for each day of winter, came to forty-seven. She had forgotten two.

Dinah did not hold with fuss, but she did hold with the shortest day. She baked a mutton pie and a dark spiced loaf with a crust like a boot. She set a lantern in the window facing the tarn, to show the sun the way back. There was a letter from Nell’s mother in the Lowlands, read twice.

After supper they went out. The lantern lay on the black ice in one long yellow stroke. “It turns tonight,” said Dinah. “You’ll not see it for a month. But it turns.”

volumes.title: Snowed In
volumes.text:
The snow came to High Ouzel in mid January and went on for three days without drawing breath. When it stopped, the yard wall was a soft white rise, the tarn had vanished, and the kitchen window was half blue.

Nell Garth, eleven, and her great-aunt Dinah dug a trench to the byre, shoulder deep to Nell, and for a week that trench was the world: house, cow, hens, house. Nobody came up from Emberwick. Nobody could. Dinah seemed to find this restful.

In the evenings she taught Nell to turn a stocking heel, which took four tries, and they played draughts on a board scratched into the table, with white buttons and black. Dinah won eleven games running. She did not let a child win, she said; it gave them wrong ideas. Nell won the twelfth, properly. Dinah made her hot milk with treacle and said nothing.

volumes.title: The Ewe Under the Drift
volumes.text:
When the January snow settled, Great-Aunt Dinah counted her ewes in the walled field above the tarn and made it fifty-nine, not sixty. Then she whistled for old Captain, two winters retired, and he got up off the hearth as if he had only been waiting.

He went along the top wall nose down and stopped at a drift as high as Nell Garth’s head. There was a round hole in it, yellow at the rim, with warm air coming out. Dinah dug. Nell, who was eleven and wanted to help, stepped forward and went in to her armpits.

So it was Nell who met the ewe first, face to face in a little blue cave, chewing, and not at all grateful. The ewe walked out over her and went to the hay. Nell was hauled out by the collar, soaked to the skin, and laughing too much to stand.

volumes.title: The Tarn Talks
volumes.text:
In February the frost came down hard on High Ouzel and stayed nine nights. On the tenth morning Great-Aunt Dinah took the axe to the tarn’s edge, chopped a hole, measured the ice against her hand, and said to Nell Garth, “Now I’ll say.”

Nell had waited since November. She went out in her iron-shod clogs, close along the shore where Dinah showed her, and found she could slide twenty yards at a push. She slid until the day went pink. Dinah watched from the bank with folded arms, then walked out and slid past her, upright as a post.

That night Nell woke. Below, the tarn was talking: a long low boom, then a twang like a fiddle string, running from shore to shore. She was not frightened. Dinah had told her. It was only the ice making room for itself, and she lay and listened.

volumes.title: The Lid Comes Off
volumes.text:
The thaw at High Ouzel began on the first of March with a drip from the byre roof and did not stop for a fortnight. The trench Nell Garth had helped dig in January became a ditch, then a stream. The yard was mud to the ankle, and it came indoors on four paws and two pairs of clogs, however Great-Aunt Dinah stood guard with the broom.

Nell was eleven and had liked the snow. She did not like this. Her stockings were never dry. The hens sulked, and the tarn below the farm had gone the grey of old porridge, with water on the ice.

Then a west wind blew all one night, and by morning the ice was gone, every plate of it, and the tarn was moving again, blue and wrinkled. Dinah stood at the door with her tea. “There,” she said. “That’s the lid off.”

volumes.title: The First Lamb
volumes.text:
The first lamb at High Ouzel was born on the nineteenth of March, at a quarter to five, in the field by the tarn. Nell Garth, eleven, was there because her great-aunt Dinah had shaken her foot through the blanket and said, “Lantern.”

There was little to do but hold the light steady. Nell used both hands. The ewe managed the rest, and then there was a wet yellowish thing on the grass that sneezed, shook its ears, and in ten minutes stood on four legs that did not agree with each other.

Dinah said the first lamb was Nell’s to name. Nell thought of the byre door and her chalk marks, one for each day of winter. She had made none for three weeks. She had forgotten to count. “Chalk,” she said. Dinah looked at the lamb, which was dark as a wet slate, and said that would do.

volumes.title: The Ouzel Comes Back
volumes.text:
On the last Thursday of March a bird sang from the rowan by Ouzel Tarn: three clear notes, a pause, and three again. Nell Garth ran down in her clogs. It was black as a blackbird, with a white bib like a tucked-in napkin. Her great-aunt Dinah came to the wall and listened, eyes shut. “That’s him,” she said. “That’s winter done.”

The carrier’s cart came to the last gate on Saturday. Nell’s mother had written that the sister in the Lowlands was well again. Dinah took the town boots down from their nail. Nell could not get her heel in.

So she went home to Emberwick in the clogs, ringing down the track. Dinah carried the box to the gate. “Lambs want marking in June,” she said, looking at the fell. “If you’ve nothing on.” She never did wash Nell’s chalk marks off the byre door.
